Lick Recon taken 09/01/2009: Rapidly Rotating at 45km/s 44Sp-hi090901.pdf TCERT 09Aug25: single transit; get classification Classification of one Lick spectrum: Teff=6250, log(g)=3.5, Vrot=50 The lines are too broad to allow precise velocities, but there is a hint in the correlation against a non-rotating template that the spectrum may be double-lined. We should get another spectrum to check on this. 44C-lb20090925.ps Lick observation phase=12.87 McD 27/28 Apr 2010 Teff=5750 K, log(g)=3.5, Vrot=50 km/s, Vrad=-8.259 km/s, phase=0.23 44C-sq20120727a.ps The Lick velocity (from Howard) is -4.339 km/s. Because of the rotation (and the weakness of the McD spectrum), the velocities are uncertain, and the variation probably isn't significant. I don't see convincing evidence of double lines, because this new spectrum is noisy and I don't trust the shoulders to the correlation peak. I don't think this warrants more recon right now. An image taken with the Lick Observatory 1-m Nickel Telescope is available in .pdf and .fits format. Each pdf has a 1.2'x1.2' view centered on the star, and a close-up view of the star in an 11"x11" field. The seeing is ~ 1.5". Close companion visible ~3" to the SE about 4 magnitudes fainter. 44Ic-hi20100711.pdf The three transits seen through Q3 shows dramatic transit depth diminishing. Also the Vsini = 50 km/s for a Teff=5700 implies tidal spin up. Perhaps some inner companion is spinning up the star and causing precession of the outer planet that is results in diminishing transit depth. The Raw and Corrected light curves from MAST do not show (by eye) any indication of the transit depths diminishing. (A plot of the unfolded light curve is shown in the "Files : Light_curves" section). The transit width is quite wide, around 20 hours. Could be a giant? The very different transit depths between the Raw and Corrected data is worrisome, and again indicates the Corrected data should never be used. The Corrected data has much smaller transit depths, implying smaller planets - scary. FOP KOI review: Bryson analysis failed for Q3; no other quarters on FOP website. LightCurve Transits appear to change depth between quarters in "corrected" data. This is probably an artifact of the processing, since the raw lightcurves show constant transit depths. The corrected lightcurves show several strange features at the locations of transits. Did the processing get messed up because of the long transit duration (~20 hours)? See Bill Welsh's plot: 44Lp-ww20120727c.png KFOP website has period of 9.43459d. Where did this come from? Certainly not from the lightcurve! KSAS has 66.51263d period which agrees with lightcurve. recon: Rapid rotator 50 km/sec Lick Recon taken 09/01/2009: Rapidly Rotating at 45km/s McD: Teff=5750 K, log(g)=3.5, Vrot=50 km/s, Vrad=-8.259 km/s, phase=0.23 At Kmag=13.48, probably too faint for Doppler tomography imaging: no A/O Lick image shows companion 3" to SE, 3 mag fainter Close companion visible ~3" to the SE about 4 magnitudes fainter. centroid pixel offset .047 pixels = 31.4 sigma model predicts 22.4 sigma offset pixel images and centroid look OK inconclusive... We need to understand the lightcurve effects, and then have TCERT take another look at this one. Rating: 2 A fit to the transits show no sign of any change in depth. The depth is 1.2% and the width is 19 hours, and the period is 66.47 days. The O-C of the transit times shows no significant variation; peak-to-peak change of only 4 minutes. However, there are only 6 transits, so this is too few transits to say very much, other than there are no obvious period changes. Revised ephemeris: To=2454993.47419 P=66.46774 days. WIYN speckle imaging was taken of K00044 on 2011-09-08. The 2.8x2.8 arcsec FOV was centered on the target star. No secondary sources were detected. See separate plots/tables for the limiting magnitude of the field as a function of distance from the target star. Observed with TRES on 20130623 UT with phase ~0.17 Robo-AO i-band imaging of KOI-44 on 2012-07-16 No companions detected within 2.5" http://arxiv.org/abs/1312.4958 I think this is a case where the alternate detrending has wiped out the secondary. I have seen that before when the period is a month or two. The DV secondary is convincing. It's weak, but not weak enough to be a planet. The period is too long to have a chance of seeing any reflected light. If you look at the very first title page, you can guess already that there is a secondary, namely DV found it for the -02 TCE. So, check "secondary observed" and "Secondary is self-lum." So, this is a small star eclipsing the target. The puzzling thing is the rapid rotation, Vrot=55 km/s. If the spin of the star is synchronized to the orbit and we are viewing the spin equator-on, then the stellar radius would have to be (55/2) x (66/25.4) = 71 times bigger than the Sun. The spectroscopic gravity is no weaker than log(g) = 2.5, so that implies a radius only 10 times bigger than the Sun. The only way out is to have another stellar companion in a tight orbit of a few days that has spun up the target. If the target really is a giant, we wouldn't expect to see light from a main-sequence inner stellar companion. And here is the interesting part. An early observations from McDonald gave an RV of -9 km/s. Gil's TRES spectrum has RV = -26 km/s. This is convincing evidence for a stellar companion of some sort, either the companion causing the transit with period 66 days, or an inner companion. In any case, the companion causing the light-curve dip is self luminous and therefore a star. TCERT 100609: Exerpt from Tim Brown's discussion of stellar radii determination Thinking about KOI-17 (see discussion at 29 Sep TCERT meeting), we discussed the anomalously high surface gravities returned by spectral synthesis (inconsistent with stellar radius from light-curve modeling). We again discussed the interplay between metallicity and surface gravity, keeping in mind that KOI-17 has a high metallicity. NB asked Tim about the sensitivity of the stellar radius and mass results (from mean-density/isochrone fits) to errors in metallicity. TB tested this and the rule was generally about a 0.5% error in radius/mass for every 0.1 dex error in metallicity (i.e. not very sensitive). HIRES Velocities to date for K00017.
